issues.legal_issue: A member’s prior appearance for one side in related proceedings can make a quasi-judicial disciplinary tribunal improperly constituted where it creates a reasonable apprehension of bias, even without proof that the member was actually biased or influenced the decision.
material_facts: The tribunal chair had appeared for the complainant in proceedings arising from the same underlying dispute.
The chair served on the tribunal hearing the professional-misconduct complaint and acted as its chair.
issues.conclusion: The chair’s prior appearance created a serious infirmity in the tribunal’s constitution because a litigant could reasonably apprehend that the chair’s connection might have operated against the advocate.
issues.legal_principle: Every member of a tribunal deciding issues judicially or quasi-judicially must be able to act impartially and objectively. The test is whether a litigant could reasonably apprehend that bias might have operated against them, not whether actual bias or influence is proved; justice must appear to be done. The Court relied on Frome United Breweries Co. v. Bath Justices, Rex v. Sussex Justices, Ex parte McCarthy, and Rex v. Essex Justices, Ex parte Perkins, and explained Rex v. Williams, Ex parte Phillips.

predicates.quasi_judicial_disciplinary_inquiry: A tribunal conducted an inquiry that required it to decide a professional-misconduct matter judicially or quasi-judicially.
predicates.tribunal_member_previously_appeared_for_: A member of the tribunal had previously appeared for the opposing side in related proceedings.
predicates.reasonable_apprehension_of_bias: The member’s prior connection could reasonably cause a litigant to apprehend that bias might operate against them.

issues.definition: If a quasi-judicial disciplinary inquiry includes a member who previously appeared for the opposing side in related proceedings and that connection creates a reasonable apprehension of bias, the tribunal is improperly constituted.

issues.legal_issue: A party waives an objection to a tribunal member’s disqualification by failing to raise it before the tribunal when the party knew the material facts and was aware, or must be treated as aware, of the right to object.
material_facts: The advocate knew that the tribunal chair had appeared for the complainant in the related proceedings.
The advocate did not object to the chair’s participation before the tribunal, but raised the objection later.
The advocate had substantial experience at the Bar and legal assistance in the proceedings; the Court rejected the claim that he was unaware of his right to object.
issues.conclusion: The advocate waived the objection and could not rely on the tribunal’s defective constitution to challenge the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Waiver cannot be inferred merely from failure to object: the party must know the relevant facts and be aware of the right to object. The Court relied on Vyvyan v. Vyvyan and held that the advocate knew the relevant facts and must be deemed conscious of his legal rights.

rule.if: tribunal_member_disqualification_objection and party_knew_relevant_facts and party_aware_of_right_to_object and party_failed_to_object_before_tribunal

predicates.tribunal_member_disqualification_objecti: A party had an objection that a tribunal member was disqualified from participating.
predicates.party_knew_relevant_facts: The party knew the facts giving rise to the claimed disqualification.
predicates.party_aware_of_right_to_object: The party was aware, or must be treated as aware, that they could object to the member’s participation.
predicates.party_failed_to_object_before_tribunal: The party did not raise the disqualification objection before the tribunal.

issues.definition: If a party knows the facts and the right underlying a disqualification objection but does not raise it before the tribunal, the objection is waived.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court’s examination of records after argument does not vitiate its decision where the examination only verifies material referred to in argument and does not contribute to the decision.
material_facts: The High Court called for and examined records after the matter had been argued.
The records were examined to verify that an application referred to during argument had in fact been made.
The reasons for the High Court’s decision showed that its examination of the records played no part in its final decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s procedure did not involve a serious irregularity warranting the setting aside of its order or a fresh hearing.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it would have considered the grievance more seriously if the High Court had relied on material documents that were not before it when the matter was argued, but found that the records did not affect the final decision.

rule.if: review_of_disciplinary_finding and records_examined_after_argument and records_only_verified_argument_reference and records_did_not_affect_decision

predicates.review_of_disciplinary_finding: A court reviewed a decision arising from a professional-misconduct inquiry.
predicates.records_examined_after_argument: The reviewing court examined records after the matter had been argued.
predicates.records_only_verified_argument_reference: The records were examined only to verify material that had been referred to during argument.
predicates.records_did_not_affect_decision: The reviewing court’s reasons showed that the records played no part in its final decision.

issues.definition: If a court reviewing a disciplinary finding examines records after argument only to verify a matter raised in argument and those records do not affect its decision, there is no serious procedural irregularity.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to examine a witness who is no better than an accomplice does not justify an adverse inference against the prosecution where the prosecutor acts bona fide in deciding which witnesses are necessary.
material_facts: The complainant did not call a court employee who had been involved in preparing the false order.
The Court considered that employee no better than an accomplice.
The Court found no basis to infer that the complainant’s decision not to call the employee was unfair or improper.
issues.conclusion: No adverse inference should be drawn against the complainant’s case from the failure to examine that witness.
issues.legal_principle: Even in quasi-criminal proceedings, important and relevant evidence must be placed before the tribunal, but the prosecutor generally decides which witnesses are necessary to unfold the case. If the prosecutor acts bona fide and fairly, a court will generally be reluctant to draw an adverse inference; failure to call a witness who is no better than an accomplice does not justify such an inference.

rule.if: quasi_criminal_proceeding and prosecutor_failed_to_call_witness and witness_no_better_than_accomplice and prosecutor_acted_bona_fide

predicates.quasi_criminal_proceeding: The matter was a quasi-criminal proceeding.
predicates.prosecutor_failed_to_call_witness: The prosecutor did not call a witness whose evidence was relevant to the case.
predicates.witness_no_better_than_accomplice: The omitted witness was no better than an accomplice in the alleged wrongdoing.
predicates.prosecutor_acted_bona_fide: The prosecutor acted fairly and bona fide in deciding which witnesses were necessary.

issues.definition: If a prosecutor acting bona fide in a quasi-criminal proceeding does not call a witness who is no better than an accomplice, the omission does not warrant an adverse inference.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of professional misconduct based on circumstantial evidence warrant no interference where the circumstances are inconsistent with innocence and lead irresistibly to guilt.
material_facts: The tribunal and the High Court both found that the advocate had participated in procuring a false stay order through improper means for the benefit of his clients.
The advocate was present when the case was adjourned and later carried the envelope containing the purported order to the magistrate’s office.
The order benefited the advocate’s clients, who were not present when it was prepared, and the Court found the explanation that it was produced by mistake unreasonable.
The evidence was substantially circumstantial, and the Court considered the lower courts’ concurrent factual findings under its special-leave jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The findings of professional misconduct were supported by the circumstances, and no case was made out for interference with the High Court’s conclusions.
issues.legal_principle: A finding of guilt on circumstantial evidence requires evidence wholly inconsistent with innocence and leading irresistibly to guilt. The Court declined to re-examine concurrent factual findings in the appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_mis: A special-leave appeal challenged concurrent findings of professional misconduct by lower decision-makers.
predicates.circumstantial_evidence_inconsistent_wit: The circumstantial evidence was wholly inconsistent with the accused person’s innocence.
predicates.circumstances_lead_irresistibly_to_guilt: The circumstances led irresistibly to the conclusion that the accused person was guilty.

issues.definition: If a special-leave appeal challenges concurrent misconduct findings supported by circumstantial evidence that is inconsistent with innocence and leads irresistibly to guilt, the findings are not disturbed.

issues.legal_issue: Removal from professional practice is justified for grave misconduct involving the corruption of public officers for a client’s benefit, particularly where the practitioner has previously been disciplined for misconduct.
material_facts: The advocate was found to have helped procure a fabricated court order through improper means for the benefit of his clients.
The Court regarded the conduct as very serious and noted an earlier suspension for misappropriating client money intended for court fees.
The Court considered the obligations and reputation of the legal profession and the need for a deterrent response to such conduct.
issues.conclusion: Removal of the advocate’s name from the roll of legal practitioners was fully justified.
issues.legal_principle: The legal profession’s special status and privileges carry corresponding obligations to maintain high standards of morality and integrity. Courts should take a serious view of reprehensible professional lapses and impose deterrent orders to protect the profession from practitioners willing to corrupt public officers for clients’ benefit.

predicates.professional_discipline_appeal: An appeal concerns a sanction imposed in professional-discipline proceedings.
predicates.grave_misconduct_corrupting_public_offic: The practitioner committed grave misconduct by corrupting public officers through improper means for a client’s benefit.
predicates.need_to_protect_professional_integrity: A strong sanction is needed to protect the profession’s standards of morality and integrity.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns professional discipline, the practitioner committed grave misconduct by corrupting public officers for a client’s benefit, and professional integrity requires a strong response, removal from practice is justified.
